comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Aug hero LR sweep — results + LR scaling law.** Figures and analysis on branch [`grug-aug-lr-sweep-results`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/grug-aug-lr-sweep-results/experiments/grug/aug_lr_sweep_figs).

## Status: 122/150 cells at full budget

d512–d1536 mostly complete; the remaining ~28 are the largest/longest cells (d2048-300×/600×, d1536-600×), which crash-and-resume off temp checkpoints and are the long pole. Best paloma `macro_loss` per cell (metric used throughout):

| size | 30× | 60× | 150× | 300× | 600× |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 | 3.844 | 3.666 | 3.502 | 3.409 | 3.336 |
| d768 | 3.467 | 3.325 | 3.185 | 3.104 | 3.048 |
| d1024 | 3.153 | 3.046 | 2.938 | 2.868 | 2.813 |
| d1280 | 2.994 | 2.899 | 2.802 | 2.740 | 2.692 |
| d1536 | 2.874 | 2.790 | 2.695 | 2.636 | (partial) |
| d2048 | 2.730 | 2.651 | (partial) | (partial) | (partial) |

## Per-cell LR optimum (log-quadratic fit)

Each cell's LR sweep fits a clean parabola in `log(LR)`; the optimum `lr*` **drifts up with token budget** — ~1.0× at 30× to **~1.2–1.4× at 300×/600×** — with a mild downward shift for wider models. The 1.0× heuristic is right for short runs but under-shoots the LR for over-trained budgets.

![per-cell](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/grug-aug-lr-sweep-results/experiments/grug/aug_lr_sweep_figs/lr_sweep_percell_fit_paloma.png?raw=true)

## Learned optimal-LR power law

Fitting the per-cell `lr*` (× the May-Recipe heuristic LR) to `lr = a·tokens^b·hidden^c·batch^0.5` (batch exponent pinned):

```
lr = 34.3 · tokens^-0.346 · hidden^-0.345 · batch^0.5      R² = 0.978, median rel err 1.6%
```

![powerlaw](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/grug-aug-lr-sweep-results/experiments/grug/aug_lr_sweep_figs/lr_powerlaw_fit.png?raw=true)

## Batch-controlled collapse

Dividing out `√batch` (and `hidden^c`) collapses **all 6 model sizes onto a single `tokens^-0.346` line**, R² = 0.979 — the optimal LR is a pure token power law once width and batch are controlled for.

![collapse](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/grug-aug-lr-sweep-results/experiments/grug/aug_lr_sweep_figs/lr_batch_collapse.png?raw=true)

## vs. current heuristic, and at the d6144 / 15T target

muonh LR = `coeff·tokens^p·hidden^q·batch^0.5` (seq 8192 folded into coeff):

| | coeff | tokens exp | hidden exp |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ours (fit)** | 34.35 | **−0.346** | **−0.345** |
| **current heuristic** | 25.89 | −0.395 | −0.150 |

Two structural disagreements: ours decays **slower with tokens** (wants more LR at large budgets) and **much faster with width**. At **d6144 / 15T tokens** these nearly cancel — our law prescribes **~1.07× the heuristic's LR** (batch-independent; e.g. batch 4096 → heuristic 2.80e-3 vs ours 2.99e-3).

**Caveat:** that agreement is a coincidental cancellation, and d6144/15T is a large extrapolation — width is **3× beyond** the widest swept model (d2048) and 15T is well past the 600× budget. The `hidden^-0.345` term (the biggest disagreement) is the least-constrained; a d6144-or-wider point is needed to pin it before trusting either law at 15T.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
Marin has no way to mark a test as needing a GPU, a minimum device count, or a specific accelerator. Some accelerator tests skip invisibly in CI as a result, and the two that need real device topology were written outside pytest entirely.

`tests/test_utils.py` provides `skip_if_no_tpu` and nothing equivalent for GPUs or device counts. The root `pyproject.toml` markers are `slow`, `integration`, `data_integration`, `cluster`, `requires_cluster`, `docker`, and `manual`; none describes hardware. `tests/cluster/conftest.py` names two clusters, `MARIN_TPU_CLUSTER` and `MARIN_GPU_CLUSTER = "cw-us-east-02a"`, with no entry for the GB200 cluster `cw-us-east-08a`.

Two tests in `lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py` check the ragged all-to-all MoE backend against a dense reference and run nowhere:

```
uv run python -m pytest lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py -rs -k "ragged or granular or clip"
...
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available[ragged_all_to_all]
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_reports_positive_drop_count_in_ragged_a2a_when_over_capacity
5 passed, 2 skipped
```

They skip on `requires an even number of >=2 devices`, and forcing two CPU devices hits the next guard, `ragged_all_to_all is not implemented on XLA:CPU`. Every job in `.github/workflows/` runs on `ubuntu-latest`. The five that pass cover lowering, offset arithmetic against a NumPy simulation of the collective, and capacity clipping in isolation. None runs the real collective or the SM100 expert kernels.

The root `addopts` does not include `-rs`, so these skips never appear in CI output. A green run with full coverage and a green run with no ragged coverage look identical.

Both files that need real accelerator topology avoided pytest. `lib/iris/tests/e2e/gpu_gang_smoke.py` is a standalone `__main__` script with `--target kind|coreweave` and `--i-understand-the-cost`; it mock-labels kind nodes to simulate an NVLink domain instead of requiring one. `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ragged_ep_check.py` (PR #8549) submits a 4-GPU GB200 job, computes a pass/fail verdict, and raises on failure, but sits under `experiments/` with no scheduled caller.

Two cases need different mechanisms. A test like the levanter one needs N local devices inside the pytest process. A test like `ragged_ep_check` needs no local hardware: it submits a job whose constraint rides in `ResourceConfig.with_gpu("GB200", count=4, ...)`, so what it needs is a cluster fixture and a way to declare that the run is expensive.

#7242 delivered `tests/cluster/`, the `cluster` marker, and `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` for smokes that submit real jobs. It left open which hardware a test needs and what a test that cannot get that hardware should do.

Done when:

- A test can declare a local device requirement and skip with a named reason instead of an ad-hoc in-file guard.
- Skipped tests are visible in CI output.
- A job-submitting test can target the GB200 cluster through a fixture, and its cost is expressible on the test rather than only in the workflow.
- One existing case is ported as the reference: the levanter ragged EP tests, or `ragged_ep_check.py`.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correction to this issue's premise, found while acting on it in #8549.

It says `tests/cluster/` "covers submitting a job to a standing cluster" and that the gap is a GB200 lane and a cost tier on the existing workflow. The workflow no longer exists. #8605 deleted `.github/workflows/marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` on 2026-08-22, and its commit message gives the reason:

> Marin Cluster Smoke had zero successful scheduled runs: all 38 runs from July 17 through August 23 were cancelled around its 100-minute timeout. The workflow and its Grafana lane are deleted. The underlying tests remain directly runnable through the cluster-test runbook.

So nothing runs the `cluster` marker at all now, and this issue covers restoring a runner rather than extending one. The two other gaps it names are unaffected: there is still no way to declare a local device requirement, and `addopts` still carries no `-rs`, so skipped tests stay invisible.

One gap it named is now closed. #8549 moved the 4-GPU ragged transport gate to `tests/cluster/grug/test_ragged_ep_check.py`. That needed only a constant naming the GB200 peer, because `cw-us-east-08a` is already a federation peer of the marin hub and `target_cluster` is a `ResourceConfig` field, so `iris_client` works unchanged. No new fixture was required after all.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correcting my comment above, which was too absolute. "No workflow runs the `cluster` marker" is accurate; "accelerator tests have no automated vehicle" was not.

Scheduled GPU work does run. `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` fires daily at 10:00 UTC against `cw-us-west-04a`, sets `CANARY_ACCELERATOR: gpu`, and runs `python -m experiments.ferries.canary_ferry` on 8x H100 through Iris, with `scripts/ci/validate_canary_metrics.py` asserting the result. That is a real accelerator smoke on a daily cron. It is not pytest and carries no marker.

`iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` looks like a second GPU lane and is not one. It runs `pytest tests/test_integration_test.py -m integration` on PRs touching `lib/iris/**`, and the workflow comment says it submits "against the shared H100" — but the jobs `tests/integration_test.py` submits are `ResourceConfig.with_cpu()` with `require_accelerator=False`. It exercises a CoreWeave-hosted controller, not a GPU.

The deleted `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` had two jobs, not one. `marin-tpu-smokes` ran on the schedule; `marin-gpu-smokes` was `if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.run_gpu`, so it never ran on a cron at all. The 38 timed-out scheduled runs the deleting commit cites were the TPU job. Standing-cluster GPU tests were therefore never automatic, before or after #8605.

So the gap this issue describes is sharper than "no runner": **no pytest marker anywhere selects GPU work.** The `cluster` marker has no workflow, and the `integration` marker runs only CPU jobs. Every GPU assertion in CI today lives in the canary ferry, outside pytest.

Two facts worth having when someone picks this up. The canary already parameterizes the accelerator (`CANARY_GPU_TYPE`, documented as "H100, GH200, B200", plus `CANARY_GPU_COUNT` and `CANARY_GPU_REPLICAS`), so scheduling GPU work of a given shape from Actions is solved machinery rather than something to build. And `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` and `iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` share the concurrency group `iris-coreweave-ci-shared` because they contend for one host, so any added lane needs a capacity story and not only a config entry.

issues.body:
# Proposal: `think-budget-calibration`: evaluating whether a model spends the right amount of thinking

**Related:** #7090 (Epic: new evals for Marin — wish-list)

## 1. Summary

An eval suite that measures **compute allocation quality**, not accuracy: does the model spend tokens in proportion to (A) how hard the item is, and (B) whether it has any realistic chance of solving it at all?

Models are scored against an **oracle allocator** that knows, per item, the minimum budget at which *that model* succeeds. Headline metric is the fraction of the oracle-vs-uniform gap recovered at equal total budget, decomposed into three named failure terms.

| ID | Task | Measures | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TBC-1** | Effort–Difficulty Calibration | Does token spend track model-relative difficulty? | generation |
| **TBC-2** | Futility Detection | Does it stop early on items it cannot solve at any budget? | generation |
| **TBC-3** | Budget Self-Report Probe | Logprob-only forced choice over difficulty buckets | logprob, in-loop |

## 2. Prior work

- **OptimalThinkingBench** (arXiv 2508.13141): OverthinkingBench + UnderthinkingBench with thinking-adjusted accuracy. No model out of 33 evaluated thinking and non-thinking models is optimal on both halves. Needs an LLM judge.
- **AbstentionBench** (arXiv 2506.09038): 20 datasets of unanswerable/underspecified items. Reasoning fine-tuning degrades abstention ~24%; raising the thinking budget makes it worse.
- **TRIAGE** (arXiv 2605.13414): closest neighbour. task pool + self-calibrated budget, model commits to an ordered plan, scored against a knapsack oracle. Names the right object: abstention in AbstentionBench is a property of the *question*, but what matters is the *model–task–budget triple*.
- **TALE / L1 / SelfBudgeter**: budget-following as a control problem, not a measurement one.

All of the above evaluate frontier models, one task at a time, and mostly presuppose that the model can follow a budget instruction.

## 3. What this suite lets us test

1. **Emergence during pretraining.** Run TBC-3 across an open scaling ladder and within-run checkpoint sequences: does difficulty-awareness appear before, with, or after the ability to solve the item? This needs published intermediate checkpoints across a FLOP range, which most projects do not have.
2. **Allocation quality without budget-following.** Measure natural token spend and score it against the oracle at the same total. Requires no instruction-following, so it works on SFT-only checkpoints and on base models with few-shot CoT.
3. **Real difficulty estimation vs. surface-cue regression.** Matched pairs, equal token count and unequal solution depth, separate "spends more on hard problems" from "spends more on long prompts".
4. **The futility threshold, as a curve.** Procedural tool-required items (exact 40x40-digit multiplication, character indexing over 4k strings) parameterised by digit count give a per-model boundary for "no realistic chance with what I have", rather than a binary answerable/unanswerable label. Judge-free.
5. **Which of three failure modes a checkpoint has.** Overthinking, futility waste, and starvation are separately reported rather than collapsed into one efficiency scalar.
6. **Whether budget-following and calibration dissociate.** Declared vs. actual spend is measured separately from allocation quality, so a model can be good at one and bad at the other.

## 4. Design

**Ground truth.** For model `M`, item `i`, over budget grid `G = {64, 256, 1024, 4096}`:

```
b*_i = min { b ∈ G : M answers i correctly under budget b }   (∞ if never)
S    = { i : b*_i < ∞ }
```

`b*` is a property of the (model, item) pair, so it is recomputed per checkpoint. Report alongside intrinsic difficulty `d_i` (generator parameter, or MATH level): tracking `d_i` is a population prior; tracking `b*_i` beyond `d_i` is self-knowledge.

**Regime.** Primary is *emergent* — no budget instruction, record natural spend `a_i`, set `B = Σ a_i`, score against the oracle at that same `B`. Advisory and enforced regimes (model declares its own per-item budgets, non-binding then binding) are secondary; expect weak compliance on non-RL-trained checkpoints and report it separately from calibration.

**Item pools** (~200 each): `trivial` (overthinking probe), `ladder` (procedural, parametric difficulty), `math-levels` (external validity), `surface-control` (matched pairs — equal token count, unequal solution depth). Futility items: underspecified variants, false premise, and the tool-required sweep.

**TBC-3** is generation-free — score bucket logprobs on a fixed continuation (`Difficulty for me: {EASY|MEDIUM|HARD|IMPOSSIBLE}`) using the existing `choice_logprob` path. Metric: ρ against `b*_i`, plus AUROC of `P(IMPOSSIBLE)` against `1[b*_i = ∞]`. Verbalised self-report is a known-weak signal, but it is nearly free and the *trajectory* across checkpoints is meaningful even when the absolute level is not.

**Generator.** Reuse #7090's difficulty ladder (multi-axis vector, D1–D5 presets, procedural instances with provably correct answers). It already produces known ordinal difficulty plus programmatic grading — the expensive part. Futility items are the same generator with a premise deleted or the digit count pushed past threshold. Recommend it lives in #7090 and is imported here.

## 5. Metrics

**Headline — `η_alloc`** at total budget `B`:

```
V_oracle  = max #items solvable within B   (0-1 knapsack over S, weights b*_i)
V_uniform = |{ i : b*_i ≤ B/n }|
η_alloc   = (V_model − V_uniform) / (V_oracle − V_uniform)
```

Uniform, not random, is the right reference: the alternative to good allocation isn't random selection; it's spending the same everywhere, which is what models actually do. Also report normalized regret `(V_oracle − V_model)/V_oracle`, stable when `V_oracle ≈ V_uniform`.

**Decomposition of the gap** — same separate-the-failure-modes move as dual grading in #7090:

- **Overthinking tax** `Σ_{i∈S, correct} max(0, a_i − b*_i)` — tokens past the point of success
- **Futility waste** `Σ_{b*_i = ∞} a_i` — tokens no budget would have saved
- **Starvation loss** `|{ i∈S : a_i < b*_i }|` — items abandoned below threshold

**Supporting:** partial ρ(`a_i`, `b*_i`) controlling for `d_i`; **surface-control delta** (ρ within matched pairs only — a large drop means the model is reading prompt features, not estimating difficulty); futility detection and waste rates (adopt TRIAGE's definitions for comparability); raw accuracy always reported alongside, since `η_alloc` alone would reward answering everything in 10 tokens.

## 6. Making the sweep affordable

Naive cost is `|G| × n` full generations per checkpoint. Instead: generate one greedy trace per item at `B_max`, then for each `b ∈ G` truncate the thinking, append `\n</think>\nFinal answer:`, and generate ≤32 tokens from the cached prefix. Cost drops from `Σ_b b` to `B_max + |G|·32`.

This is s1's budget-forcing used as a measurement device, and it biases low — a truncated trace underestimates a model that natively knew it had budget `b`. **Phase 1 gate:** re-generate 50 items natively at each `b`; if rank correlation with truncation-derived `b*` is below ~0.8, drop the trick and coarsen the grid instead.

Greedy decoding throughout (`do_sample=False`), consistent with #6235. Exception: `k=4` at `t=0.7` on futility items, where a single greedy failure is weak evidence for `b*_i = ∞`.

## 7. Plan

- **Phase 0** — TBC-3 as an lm-eval-harness task on an in-house base and SFT checkpoint pair. Logprob only, no GPU. Validates harness, generator, metrics at zero generation cost.
- **Phase 1** — full emergent-regime pipeline on two external ~1–2B models that fit a free-tier T4: one hybrid-thinking model (gives thinking/non-thinking arms from one checkpoint) and one reasoning-distilled model. Validates the truncation trick; produces first `η_alloc` and decomposition.
- **Phase 2** — in-house checkpoints via the existing vLLM path. With no thinking mode available, this measures natural CoT spend under few-shot prompting — an under-reported regime.
- **Phase 3** — TBC-3 across the scaling ladder and within-run checkpoints. Plot ρ and solve rate against FLOPs on one axis. This is the part that is a paper, not a dashboard number.

## 8. Open questions

1. Is compute-priced evaluation in scope for the dashboard, or better as a standalone artifact that imports checkpoints?
2. Is there appetite for running TBC-3 across the scaling ladder? Highest-value experiment here, and the one needing maintainer compute rather than contributor compute.
3. Is a thinking-mode or RL-trained checkpoint on the roadmap? If so, the budget-following regimes become far more informative and should be designed against that target now.

comments.author: Nativeatom
comments.body:
Some details that might enrich the plan.

- The task choice might affect the budget style. If the pattern is generalizable across different tasks (or task groups), maybe starting with task with shorter budgets is a better idea (an extreme example is SWE vs simpleQA).

- How is Pt 4 in Section 3 being tested here?

- Would the budget setting limits the task choice (e.g. math reasoning), and is this preference expected?

- If budget-controlled training strategy is included in the checkpoints, the model choice should include this into consideration if accessible (even though they are beyond the budget choice).

comments.author: ayush1298
comments.body:
@Nativeatom 

**1. Task choice affecting budget style:**
Agree on starting short, disagree on assuming generalization. TRIAGE found triage quality doesn't transfer across benchmarks, so cross-family transfer should be a reported result, not a design assumption. v0 stays single-turn with ≤1k-token horizons; a second family gets added only once within-family η is stable, and transfer is measured explicitly. SWE-style agentic tasks are out of scope for v0 regardless — the budget object there is turns × tokens, not tokens, so `b*` isn't the same quantity.

**2. How Pt 4 is tested.**
The concrete test: sweep the generator's difficulty parameter n (digit count), and at each n record solve rate, mean tokens spent, and abstain rate. That gives two thresholds — `n_cap` where accuracy hits zero, and `n_behav` where spend drops or abstention rises. The metric is the **lag** `n_behav − n_cap`; a calibrated model has lag ≈ 0, and the known failure is `n_behav` sitting far past `n_cap`. Futility waste then gets restricted to `n > n_cap` rather than computed over a hand-labelled set. 

**3. Does the budget setting constrain task choice.**
Yes — it needs programmatic grading, single-turn, and an answer that's still verifiable after truncation, which pushes toward math/code/procedural. Same bias exists in UnderthinkingBench and TALE. It's expected but the domain isn't the axis that matters; "thinking pays" vs "thinking doesn't pay" is, and the `trivial` pool covers the second. Real limitation to state plainly: no free-form or long-form generation in v0, so nothing here speaks to calibration where quality isn't binary.

**4. Budget-controlled training as a covariate.**
Agree. A length-RL'd model can post good η_alloc because its spend was shaped in training, not because it estimates difficulty — so provenance has to be recorded and results stratified by it (no length control / prompt-budget SFT / length-RL). Worth including one length-controlled checkpoint deliberately, as an upper-reference arm rather than a comparison point. Sharper consequence for §3.1: if length shaping enters partway through a training run, the emergence curve across that run's checkpoints is contaminated — those sweeps need checkpoints from before the stage, or the stage boundary marked on the plot.

comments.author: mrinal-bespoke
comments.body:
I like the model-relative framing here, but I think these points need to be resolved before implementation:

1. How does Phase 0 get the `b*_i` labels without running generations? TBC-3 is scored against `b*_i`, but those labels only exist after evaluating each item over the budget grid. Should TBC-3 move after the first generation sweep, or should Phase 0 use the generator’s intrinsic difficulty `d_i` as its target?

2. How should the oracle handle non-monotonic results across budgets? A model may succeed at 256 tokens and fail at 1024, so retaining only the minimum successful budget loses information and makes the uniform baseline unreliable. Could the design retain the observed result or success probability for every `(item, budget)` pair and compute the oracle from that curve? Items with no success should be described as “unsolved within the tested grid,” rather than impossible.

3. What exactly counts as natural thinking spend `a_i`? This needs a fixed rule for models without `<think>` delimiters, responses that hit the maximum output length, and responses that produce an answer without explicit reasoning. Without that definition, the total budget `B` is not reproducible across models or checkpoints.

4. Where will the initial task pool come from? #7090 is a wishlist and does not currently provide the referenced D1–D5 generator. Could the v0 scope define one concrete task family, generator parameters and seeds, programmatic grader, item count, and matched-pair construction? That would make the first implementation and its acceptance criteria clear.

comments.author: ayush1298
comments.body:
@mrinal-bespoke thanks for the questions. All of them are relevant and below are the detailed responses to each of them: 

## 1. Phase 0 circularity

TBC-3 has two targets conflated into one task, so I will split them like: 

- **TBC-3a — intrinsic.** Target is the generator's difficulty parameter `d_i`, known at item-construction time. Generation-free, no sweep, runs in-loop. Claim: *the model has learned the population difficulty prior.*
- **TBC-3b — model-relative.** Target is the model's own success curve. Requires the sweep, so it runs after the first generation pass. Claim: *the model knows what is hard for itself.* The `P(IMPOSSIBLE)` AUROC metric also lives here, since it needs the sweep too.

Phase 0 therefore reports 3a only, and is honest about being a plumbing-and-prior check rather than a self-knowledge result. The interesting quantity — partial ρ against the success curve controlling for `d_i` — is a Phase 1 deliverable.

Consequence for the scaling-ladder experiment: 3a runs across the full ladder cheaply; 3b needs a sweep per checkpoint, so it runs on a subsample of 8–12 checkpoints spanning the FLOP range. Worth stating that the emergence plot has two curves at different resolutions rather than one.

## 2. Non-monotonicity

Agreed, and scalar `b*_i` should go. Replace it with the full curve.

For each item and each grid point, estimate `s_i(b) ∈ [0,1]` from `k` samples and retain every `(i, b)` pair. The oracle then becomes a **multiple-choice knapsack**: each item selects exactly one `b ∈ G ∪ {0}` at cost `b` and value `s_i(b)`, maximising `Σ s_i(b_i)` subject to `Σ b_i ≤ B`. Exact DP over budget discretised at the grid's gcd — no monotonicity assumption anywhere, and it's cheaper than the 0-1 formulation it replaces. `V_uniform = Σ s_i(B/n)` snapped to the nearest grid point.

Terminology fixed as you suggest: `U_G` = **unsolved within the tested grid at k samples**, with `G` and `k` stated in every table. No impossibility claim.

`b*_i` survives only as a derived reporting convenience, `argmin{b : s_i(b) ≥ 0.5}`, never as the object the oracle is computed from.

## 3. Defining `a_i`

- `a_i` = generated tokens from end of prompt to the first token of the extracted answer span, **excluding** the answer span, counted in the evaluated model's own tokenizer.
- **With `<think>` delimiters:** tokens inside the delimiters. Both figures are logged; they should agree, and a disagreement means the answer-extraction regex is wrong.
- **No explicit reasoning** (answer emitted immediately): `a_i = 0`. This is a valid measurement and the correct behaviour on trivial items, not a degenerate case.
- **Hit the cap without a parseable answer:** `a_i = cap`, `s_i(b) = 0` for that pair, flagged as truncated. **Truncation rate is reported; if it exceeds 10% at `B_max` the cap is too low and `B_max` must be raised before the run counts.**
- **Post-answer continuation:** excluded from `a_i`, logged separately as trailing tokens so total serving cost is still recoverable.
- Answer extraction is one regex per task family, owned by the grader.

Cross-model comparability: token counts are in each model's own tokenizer, so absolute `B` is not comparable across models. Within-model curves use raw tokens; cross-model comparisons normalise by that model's median spend on the trivial pool.

## 4. v0 task pool

Correct, and thanks for catching it — the D1–D5 generator was something I proposed in the wishlist thread, not something that exists. Dropping the dependency; v0 defines its own family standalone. If the proxy-benchmark generator does land later it can be upstreamed, but nothing here should block on it.

**Family: `mulcarry`** — exact integer multiplication with controlled carry structure. Chosen because one generator covers every mechanism the design needs.

- **Parameters:** `(n_digits, carry_density, seed)`. Operands are sampled to hit a target carry density at fixed digit count.
- **Why this family:** surface length is exactly `n_digits`, so difficulty and prompt length are decoupled by construction — matched pairs are trivial to build rather than curated. CoT genuinely pays (long multiplication is unreachable at 64 tokens, reachable at 1024), so the budget response is informative. Grading is exact integer comparison. And the futility sweep is the same knob pushed further, so the threshold curve needs no separate item source.
- **Grader:** strip non-digits from the extracted span, compare as integers.
- **Seeding:** items are a deterministic function of `(family, n_digits, carry_density, index)` under one published master seed; the generator reproduces the item set byte-identically.

| Pool | Parameters | Items |
|---|---|---|
| `trivial` | `n_digits ∈ {1,2}`, low carry | 60 |
| `ladder` | `n_digits ∈ {2..6} × carry_density ∈ {0.1,0.5,0.9}` | 300 |
| `surface-control` | fixed `n_digits`, `carry_density` 0.1 vs 0.9, paired | 60 pairs |
| `futility-sweep` | `n_digits ∈ {8,12,16,24,32,40}` | 150 |

~630 items. With `|G| = 4` and the truncation trick that's roughly 1.4M generated tokens per checkpoint — around 13h on a free-tier T4 at 1.5B, so a reduced smoke config (`ladder` seeds cut to 10, `|G| = 3`, ~350 items) is the default for iteration and the full config is a single overnight run.

MATH-by-level stays in the design as external validity but is explicitly **out of v0 scope**, since it brings a difficulty label we don't control and a grader we'd have to trust.

**v0 acceptance criteria:**

1. Generator reproduces the item set byte-identically from the published seed.
2. Grader agrees with hand-checking on 50 sampled traces, zero false accepts.
3. Non-monotonicity rate reported, with truncation-derived and natively-generated curves compared on a 50-item subsample.
4. `η_alloc` plus the three-term decomposition computed end-to-end on one sub-2B model.
5. Surface-control delta reported — if global ρ survives but within-pair ρ collapses, the eval is measuring prompt length and v0 has failed its own check.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
The repository pins jax 0.11.0 in seven places across marin, levanter, iris, and fray. Bumping all of them to 0.11.1 breaks grug attention, because 0.11.1 requires `dot_general` batch dimensions to carry the same sharding on both operands.

Reproduce by setting every `jax`/`jaxlib` pin to 0.11.1 and `libtpu` to `0.0.46.*` (the version 0.11.1's own `tpu` extra names), then `uv lock` and run the suite. Four tests fail on CPU with one error:

```
jax._src.core.ShardingTypeError: dot_general requires lhs batch dimensions and rhs batch
dimensions to have the same sharding, got (('replica_dcn', 'data', 'expert'), 'model')
and (('replica_dcn', 'data', 'expert'), None)
```

- `tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py::test_latent_moe_shrinks_the_dispatched_width_but_not_the_token`
- `tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py::test_hybrid_kv_branches_agree_on_sharding_when_model_axis_is_wide`
- `tests/test_grug_variant_contracts.py::test_grug_variant_one_step_contract_lowers_with_default_ctor[moe]`
- `tests/test_snowball_grug_parity.py::test_snowball_matches_grug_experiment_per_layer_and_logits`

The run used `-x`, and CPU cannot reach the GPU or TPU attention backends, so four is a lower bound rather than a count.

All four land in `reference_attention` at `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py:272`, on `jnp.einsum("bqhd,bkhd->bhqk", q * scale, k)`. The batch dimensions there are `b` and `h`. `q` carries `model` sharding on the head axis; `k` carries none, because `align_kv_heads` (`_core.py:244`) expands grouped-query KV heads with `expand_dims` + `broadcast_to` + `reshape` and the result loses the head-axis sharding. That function already carries the comment "Use reshape + broadcast instead of `jnp.repeat` to avoid sharding issues", so it has been fragile here before; 0.11.1 defeats the existing workaround.

The fix is not obviously local. Either `align_kv_heads` takes the target sharding, or `reference_attention` reshards `k` and `v` to `q`'s head spec. Both sit on the path every grug variant uses, including the TPU and GPU hero configurations, so the change needs accelerator validation and not only CPU tests. `libtpu` moving 0.0.44 to 0.0.46 alongside it widens that further.

This surfaced in #8549, where the ragged all-to-all transport forces two `XLA_FLAGS` entries that jax 0.11.0 does not define. That PR keeps a runtime guard (`RAGGED_MINIMUM_JAX_VERSION` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py`) which refuses an opt-in ragged run on a runtime below 0.11.1, rather than letting every rank abort at import on an unknown flag. The guard can go away once this lands.

Done when:

- Every `jax`/`jaxlib` pin is on the target release and `libtpu` matches what that release's `tpu` extra names.
- The four tests above pass, and the grug attention backends are validated on GPU and TPU rather than CPU alone.
- #8549's `RAGGED_MINIMUM_JAX_VERSION` guard is removed, since the pinned runtime then satisfies the flags.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Research

JAX 0.11.1 is the current stable PyPI release. The workspace still has seven 0.11.0 runtime pins across [Levanter](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/pyproject.toml#L83-L112), [Marin](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/pyproject.toml#L117-L151), [Iris](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/pyproject.toml#L70-L83), and [Fray](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/fray/pyproject.toml#L20-L24). In [reference_attention](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py#L250-L275), grouped-query expansion leaves K/V heads unsharded while Q heads use `model`; JAX 0.11.1 rejects those unequal `dot_general` batch-dimension shardings.

Proposed Fix

Bump all runtime pins to JAX/JAXlib 0.11.1 and libtpu 0.0.46, regenerate the lock, and reshard expanded K/V batch dimensions to match Q before both attention contractions. Add an explicit-mesh regression that lowers grouped-query reference attention with a model-sharded query. PR #8549 is the only overlapping work found; its version guard remains scoped to that open branch and can be removed there after this upgrade lands.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body: 🤖 Implemented in #8716. All JAX/JAXlib pins move to 0.11.1 and libtpu moves to 0.0.46; expanded K/V tensors now match Q's batch/head sharding before reference-attention contractions. The four reported CPU failures pass, along with [three v6e-4 splash cases](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fjax-0111-grug-tpu-final-8715) and [six H100 FA4 CuTe parity cases](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fjax-0111-grug-gpu-final-8715). The change reuses #8709's adjacent score-sharding fix; #8549 can remove its runtime-version guard after the upgrade lands.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body: 🤖 #8716 remains open after the 12-hour monitoring window. CI is green and GitHub reports the branch mergeable; maintainer review is still required. The standard profiled H100 canary remains blocked by the pre-existing post-profile CUDA launch failure documented on the PR, while the final-tree H100 FA4 CuTe and v4/v6e splash parity jobs passed.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
Four-stage explicit-MPMD JaxPP training can deadlock before the first loss when `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` uses the JAX 0.11 device-initiated NCCL path. The same nightly stack completes an exact-ring pipeline control, and the device ragged collective is bitwise exact and `7.4349x` faster in a direct EP8 benchmark. This blocks using the public device collective for the L24 pipeline target tracked in #7024.

Reproduce:
1. Check out [`0cabe5f74b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec).
2. Run the [four-H100 lower-bound command](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/experiments/grug/moe/repro_jaxpp_jax011_ragged_all_to_all.README.md#h100-command). Direct ragged-all-to-all, JaxPP transfer, and their minimum two-rank composition all return exactly with checksum `202`.
3. Launch `experiments/grug/moe/run_cw_jaxpp_may_d2560.sh` on four H100x8 ranks with JAX/JAXLIB/CUDA13 plugin/PJRT `0.11.1.dev20260725`, NCCL `2.30.7`, JaxPP `7091a9b5ce02cd1a6bdc905f6a36e89370a5fba9`, L8/d2560/e64/top-k4/seq4096/b512/m16, four two-layer stages, `ragged_all_to_all`, reference attention, XLA expert GEMM, and XLA autotuning/GEMM rewrites disabled.
4. Use either GPipe or standard 1F1B with `transfer_priority`. The known runs are `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260726-111423` and `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260726-113121`.

GPipe stops with rank 0 in `enqueue_nccl_transfer_group -> ncclGroupEnd`, ranks 1-2 in `recv_done_impl`, and rank 3 in `backend_compile_and_load`. Transfer-priority 1F1B stops with ranks 0-1 in DIME `enqueue_nccl_transfer_group`, rank 2 compiling, and rank 3 in PJRT execution. Both hold about `56.8-57.6 GiB` per active GPU with 0% memory activity and emit no loss or MFU. The [research logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/.agents/logbooks/jaxpp-grug-moe.md#2026-07-26-0450-pdt---gpipe-and-transfer-priority-retain-the-device-ragged-deadlock) records the controls and full rank evidence.

Expected: all four ranks complete finite training steps, or JaxPP reports a bounded coordination error instead of waiting indefinitely in mixed transfer, compile, and execution states.

The minimum primitive composition passes, so the smallest known failing boundary still includes the four-stage training graph. This package is ready to adapt for an upstream report, but no NVIDIA issue has been filed.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Actionability check — issue is well-specified (pins, run IDs, isolation matrix), keep as tracking issue
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (#7024 tracks the thread; PR #7079 is FP8, not this deadlock)
- [x] Root-cause analysis + proposed approach
- [x] Scope decision: no self-contained Marin fix → analysis comment, no PR

# Research

The hang is in the JAX `0.11.1.dev20260725` **device-initiated NCCL path**, triggered only when JaxPP's explicit inter-stage DIME transfers coexist with device `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` in the four-stage MoE graph. It is not a Marin logic bug and not fixable in-repo. The isolation matrix in the logbook pins the boundary:

- Direct device `ragged_all_to_all` on two H100s: **exact**, checksum `202`, `7.4349x` faster than the host path.
- JaxPP transfer-only control and the two-rank transfer+ragged composition: **pass**.
- Matched nightly **exact-ring** pipeline (no explicit ragged transfer): **4/4**, finite loss `8.797631`.
- Four-stage device-ragged + JaxPP transfer: **deadlocks** under GPipe, standard 1F1B, and transfer-priority alike — ranks split across `enqueue_nccl_transfer_group → ncclGroupEnd`, `recv_done_impl`, `backend_compile_and_load`, and PJRT execution; ~57 GiB held per GPU at 0% memory activity, no loss/MFU.

So the smallest known failing boundary is the full four-stage training graph; every reduced schedule and the primitive composition pass. The device NCCL communicator setup also required pinning `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.7` to clear a `ncclDevCommCreate` segfault, and autotuning/GEMM rewrites had to be disabled to reach the transfer stage — after which execution deadlocks.

**Relevant code** (branch `research/jaxpp-grug-moe` @ `0cabe5f74b`, tracks #7024):
- [`ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L77`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L77) / [`#L105`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L105) — dispatch/combine device collective
- [`repro_jaxpp_jax011_ragged_all_to_all.README.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/experiments/grug/moe/repro_jaxpp_jax011_ragged_all_to_all.README.md) — two-rank primitive boundary (passes)
- [`jaxpp_jax_0_11_inline.patch`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/experiments/grug/moe/jaxpp_jax_0_11_inline.patch) — JaxPP↔JAX 0.11 compat shim
- [logbook 04:50 PDT](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/.agents/logbooks/jaxpp-grug-moe.md#2026-07-26-0450-pdt---gpipe-and-transfer-priority-retain-the-device-ragged-deadlock) — full rank evidence

# Proposed approach

No Marin code change resolves this — the deadlock is in the JAX/NCCL/JaxPP device-collective stack. Recommend two independent tracks for a human to sign off on:

1. **File upstream.** The two-rank reproducer already isolates the transfer+ragged composition and passes, while the four-stage graph hangs; that is the evidence an upstream bug needs. File against JaxPP (NVIDIA) and/or JAX with the pinned environment and the mixed-state rank dump, and link it back here. The issue notes the package is "ready to adapt for an upstream report" but none is filed yet.
2. **Unblock #7024 in the interim.** The nightly **exact-ring** pipeline completes 4/4 with finite loss, so the L24 target is not gated on the device collective. Fall back to the exact-ring transfer path (accepting the ~7.4x transport loss on `ragged_all_to_all`) until upstream fixes the device path, rather than blocking pipeline-parallel MoE training on it.

I am not opening a PR: the fix is upstream and the in-repo decision (upstream report vs. exact-ring fallback for #7024) needs a human owner.

issues.title: [grug] JaxPP device-ragged pipelines deadlock during DIME transfer

issues.author: claude[bot]
issues.body:
The Tier-1 datakit smoke ferry failed. The `datakit-smoke/verify_fuzzy_dups` step raised, propagated through `StepRunner` (`RuntimeError: 1 step(s) failed`), and failed the ferry job. The driver runs with `max_task_failures=0`, so a single step failure fails the canary.

Root cause: `verify_fuzzy_dups` loads a distributed in-memory document store. A verify worker was preempted and restarted mid-run (worker 66 reached `attempt=1` and reinstalled its venv at 08:50) on the preemptible v4 pool. When the memory-store load poll re-resolved to the restarted actor, that actor no longer held the in-flight operation, so Iris returned `ConnectError: Operation '94446ed7…' not found` (`Code.NOT_FOUND`). `is_retryable_error` classifies `NOT_FOUND` as a non-retryable application error (`lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/errors.py:135`), and `actor_result_with_recovery` only recovers `TimeoutError` and `ActorUnavailableError` (`lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/memory_store.py:301-314`). The `NOT_FOUND` therefore propagates and fails the step.

Reproduce:
1. Run `experiments.ferries.datakit_ferry` on preemptible TPU workers.
2. Preempt or restart a verify worker while `verify_fuzzy_dups` is in its memory-store load pass.
3. The load poll re-resolves to the restarted actor, which returns `NOT_FOUND` for the in-flight operation, and the step fails.

Expected: A memory-store actor restart during the load pass should re-issue the load against the recovered actor, the way `ActorUnavailableError` already triggers re-issue in `actor_result_with_recovery`. An operation lost to an actor restart is recoverable, not fatal.

<details>
<summary>Trimmed traceback (driver task 0)</summary>

```
File "lib/marin/src/marin/processing/classification/deduplication/verify_fuzzy_dups.py", line 835, in verify_fuzzy_dups
    document_store = ctx.load_memory_store(...)
File "lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py", line 407, in load_pass
    actor_result_with_recovery(...)
File "lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/memory_store.py", line 300, in actor_result_with_recovery
    return future.result(timeout=max(0.0, remaining))
File "lib/fray/src/fray/iris_backend.py", line 413, in result
    op = self._client.poll_operation_status(self._op_id)
File "lib/iris/src/iris/actor/client.py", line 183, in poll_operation_status
File "lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/actor_connect.py", line 482, in get_operation
connectrpc.errors.ConnectError: Operation '94446ed71a9743a997e75ec1a9966e23' not found

RuntimeError: Step failed: datakit-smoke/verify_fuzzy_dups_8a99f4b7
RuntimeError: 1 step(s) failed
```
</details>

Evidence:
- `iris job describe /runner/iris-run-job-20260824-073906`: `State: failed`, `failures=1`, `Error: RuntimeError: 1 step(s) failed`; task 0 ran 1h16m.
- Verify worker 66 reached `attempt=1` and reinstalled its venv at 08:50, consistent with preemption and reschedule on the preemptible v4 pool.
- Distinct from the wait-budget overruns in #8580, #8529, and #8273: this job failed at 1h16m, well under the 7100s wait budget.

## Canary run context

- Lane: datakit-smoke (Tier 1, TPU / GCP)
- Iris job ID: `/runner/iris-run-job-20260824-073906`
- GHA run: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/32702408963
- Run ID: `datakit-smoke-32702408963-1`
- W&B: `marin-community/marin` (datakit smoke does not create a per-run W&B run)

comments.body:
🤖 Recurrence of this failure on the Tier-1 datakit smoke canary, 3 days after the original report.

The run failed in `datakit-smoke/verify_fuzzy_dups` at ~1h17m wall-clock, well under the 7100s wait budget, with the recorded job failure reason being a `max_task_failures` trip, on the heavily-preempted preemptible-v4 pool. Same fingerprint as the original report (failure in verify, ~1h16m, under budget, preemption-driven), and distinct from the wait-budget timeouts in #8580 (which fail during consolidate/tokenize with `TimeoutError`, not a step failure).

**Caveat:** I could not fetch the driver task-0 traceback for this run to confirm the exact `ConnectError: Operation ... not found`. The verify driver/coordinator process logs live in Finelog and `iris process logs`, both approval-gated in the triage runner, and the collected diagnostics bundle only captured the ~19:02-19:10 UTC teardown window, so the active verify window and the driver crash are not in it. The attribution below is from the job tree, stage timing, and failure reason.

**Canary run context**
- Lane: datakit-smoke (Tier 1, GCP / preemptible v4, us-central2)
- Iris job ID: `/runner/iris-run-job-20260827-175226`
- GHA run: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/33100523894
- Run ID: `datakit-smoke-33100523894-1`
- Date: 2026-08-27

**Evidence**
- Timeline: job submitted 17:52:29 UTC, verify stage started 18:53, torn down ~19:09, so ~1h17m, matching the original ~1h16m and well under the 7100s (~118 min) budget. Not a 8580-style timeout, and the pipeline never reached consolidate/tokenize.
- The five `fuzzy-dups-59865998` coordinator waves (18:19-18:50) are the expected iterative connected-components behavior established in #8580, not a crash loop.
- The ferry driver runs with `max_task_failures=0` (`lib/fray/src/fray/types.py:723`), so a single verify step failure fails the whole canary, consistent with the truncated root reason `Cumulative failed task attempts exceeded max_task_failures`.
- Heavy preemptible-TPU churn during the window (repeated `worker reconcile failure threshold exceeded`, slice terminations, GCP no-more-capacity-in-zone in the controller logs), i.e. the preemption conditions that trigger the memory-store `NOT_FOUND` recovery gap in `actor_result_with_recovery` (`lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/memory_store.py:301-314`).

The fix proposed in the original report still stands: re-issue the memory-store load against the recovered actor on `NOT_FOUND`, the way `ActorUnavailableError` already triggers re-issue.

Note: the ferry sets `FuzzyVerificationStoreConfig(recovery_timeout=1800, ready_timeout=1800)` for verify. Those timeouts do not cover the `NOT_FOUND` path, which is classified non-retryable (`lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/errors.py:135`) and bypasses the recovery wait entirely.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
The Marin codebase needs to maintain a high level of quality to preserve development velocity. As agents have increased the rate of code production, the burden of doing code reviews has increased as well. While we don't demand code review for every PR, we still rely on it for important new code additions and to ensure code fits our guidelines.

One area we're particularly concerned about is slop. Agents produce "slop" in a way and scope well beyond a normal human coder: documentation or comments written in a bizarre style, oddly baroque abstractions, or repetitive coding practices. As a reviewer, it's frustrating and tiring to have to comment on slop code.

We have an initial set of agentic linting rules tied into our commit process that were mostly created from scratch. This proposes a weekly process to automatically refine and improve these rules based on observed reviewer feedback: rules which have never triggered are removed, and new rules introduced to capture common patterns, measured automatically and rolled out against a benchmarking set to ensure we don't regress.

## Current status

Our review process tracks findings by rule and user. Currently 3,672 findings across 61 distinct rules; the top 12 rules account for ~62% of findings, with the remaining 49 rules accounting for 37.4% (1,373).

Top rules by finding count:

| Rule | Findings | Share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| ml-tuple-return-shape | 285 | 7.8% |
| ml-duplicate-logic-block | 277 | 7.5% |
| ml-magic-constant | 245 | 6.7% |
| ml-overloaded-function | 245 | 6.7% |
| ml-impl-narration-docstring | 244 | 6.6% |
| ml-slop-test | 243 | 6.6% |
| ml-unused-param | 216 | 5.9% |
| ml-echo-across-files | 154 | 4.2% |
| ml-module-globals | 108 | 2.9% |
| ml-env-var-vs-param | 97 | 2.6% |
| ml-duplicate-constant | 93 | 2.5% |
| ml-misleading-name | 92 | 2.5% |
| Remaining 49 rules | 1,373 | 37.4% |

A spot review shows these reviews are almost always acted on by the development agent, implying even the ad-hoc reviews have saved thousands of user interactions. Despite this, we still regularly post PRs full of agentic slop, with plenty of room for improvement.

## Proposal

Two levers:

- **Better enforcement:** auto-reject PRs that don't have the `agentic-review` tag assigned to them. This should force agents that forgot the agentic review process to trigger review.
- **Better quality:** every human comment on a PR is something that *could* have been caught during agentic PR review. Analyze these weekly and identify the comment types that recur most frequently and are easiest to resolve.

## Approach

- Move statistics out of WandB and into Finelog via a bulk import & CLI adjustments
- Add a Grafana dashboard for monitoring & alerting rules as appropriate
- Set up a weekly GitHub action which:
  - **Fetch:** all PRs with comments in the last week
  - **Triage:** which comments are actionable for linting
  - **Review:** which rules haven't fired for > 1 month
  - **Adopt:** new rules which would have captured the failure patterns

## Success criteria

- A live dashboard on Grafana showing agentic code review feedback statistics, including triggers, feedback quality metrics, timing (too slow a feedback loop and users get impatient), and any issues we run into
- Weekly report sent to Slack with our PR statistics
- A codified, tentatively weekly, auto-improvement process for our agentic linting patterns

Long-term success metric: *does the number of PR comments that could have been caught by agentic linting go down over time?* This is not a hard metric — it will fluctuate as coding standards change and as agents get more powerful — but in general we want to see it go down.

## Rollout

Bulk upload of all agentic lint data into Finelog with the initial rollout, then set up GitHub actions for the maintenance loop.

## Expected timeframe

~1 day of work, which can be overlapped with other ongoing projects.

## Alternatives considered

**Do nothing.** Rejected: this is a low-effort way to reduce human reviewer load.

**Adopt some external service.** Rejected: lack of a self-reinforcement cycle, and an initial survey found no external service provided significantly higher value.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## Background

Finelog is our ingestion and query service for logs, metrics and telemetry. Nearly all of our logging data is sent to finelog for stable storage. Each cluster runs a finelog server for tasks running on that cluster; per-cluster data is forwarded to the shared finelog *hub*, which also serves queries for Iris (log fetching, RPC stats, host memory usage, etc.) and Grafana.

Finelog has grown organically, which has exposed a few design problems:

- Finelog writes to local SSD first, then archives to GCS. Once objects age out of local storage they are no longer queryable via the finelog server and must be queried manually.
- Finelog does not strongly separate telemetry (periodically sampled, strongly typed data, e.g. from training runs) from logs (unstructured, time-ordered log lines).
- Indexing, partitioning and query optimization are ad-hoc.

Together these produce occasionally slow or hard-to-optimize queries, and unnecessary load on the finelog server that could be offloaded to clients. Maintaining and hand-optimizing this takes time away from more productive work.

## Proposal

Move Finelog to be "object store first": write records and compact directly to the object store, and use the transition as an opportunity to fix partitioning and indexing.

The finelog server remains the primary ingestion path and the query path for ad-hoc queries, but the new model adds *client directed queries*: clients can request the *catalog* from the finelog server (all segments, their indices, and the partitioning scheme) and use it to issue direct reads against stored segments. This removes finelog as a scaling bottleneck for queries and as a source of failure.

## Success criteria

- No longer stages to local disk (we may optionally stage L0 shards if going straight to the object store is a problem).
- A comprehensive schema policy framework for describing a *schema* (a typed set of records):
  - how data in the schema is partitioned (hive partitioning by date, etc.)
  - what indices to construct
  - sort & grouping order for segments
- The Finelog client supports both `server` and `client` based query models, with the client resolving directly against GCS objects.
- A reusable migration model for online updates of existing schemas without downtime — e.g. changing hive partitioning to introduce year/month/date bucketing.
- Performance comparable to the current setup for our Grafana dashboards.

## Approach

Mostly extending and improving existing features. New pieces:

**Per-schema policy registration.** A clean mechanism to describe ingestion, compaction, partitioning and indexing plans for a schema. For example, levanter metrics might be hive-partitioned by month and day, sorted by `{run-id, feature, seq-id}`, and indexed on run-id. This enables efficient "what are all of the run-ids" queries, a natural query retirement policy (drop older dates), and efficient lookup of per-feature series.

**Online migration.** Extending a schema is "free" today (adding columns doesn't perturb existing segments), but removing indices or changing partitioning is not and currently requires careful manual migration. Borrowing from Postgres, we'll use a primitive MVCC mechanism: versioning plus dual writes make migration safe and incremental. A schema or partition break triggers a new Finelog version; multiple versions can be active for ingestion but only one is active for querying at a time. Once bulk older segments are migrated, the query version is flipped and the older version can be deleted.

**Cleaning up objects.** Making GCS canonical means we also need to clean it up: existing GCS artifacts are archival only and don't necessarily follow the same indexing or clustering policies as live objects. We propose a one-time archival of these old objects for safe-keeping, as they are rarely/never queried today. Going forward all objects are kept in a maintained state, and since the object store is globally accessible we can use e.g. Iris jobs for bulk maintenance events.

## Rollout

We want to do this migration once, so we'll test locally and on `marin-dev` before final deployment. Many of the required features already exist: if we only wanted to offload to object storage, we could likely do so simply by changing our output disk targets and measuring the performance effect.

## Expected timeframe

~1 week of work, overlappable with other ongoing projects. Most of the work is in validation and rollout.

## Alternatives considered

- **Do nothing**, and just bump disk size and schema size limits to allow deeper queries. Rejected as a long-term fix: it results in increasingly expensive queries and periodic manual maintenance events to bump disk volume size.
- **Adopt an alternative ingestion engine**, e.g. [Lance](https://lancedb.github.io/lance/) or [Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/), both of which appear to be mature log/metric service engines. Since fixing Finelog to have effectively unbounded capacity looks like a relatively small amount of work, and it supports the exact tuning and patterns we use, we defer adoption of these for later.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Assessment:** design proposal, not a bug fix. This spans the Rust store, policy/migration framework, the Python client, and deploy/archival, and the author scopes it at ~1 week. Per the fix-issue workflow I'm not opening a PR; below is a current-state map plus a proposed decomposition for review. The main finding: most of the required machinery already exists, so this is largely extension + a rollout, not greenfield.

**Current state vs. the five success criteria**

- *No local-disk staging.* Today the store is local-first with a `LOCAL -> BOTH -> REMOTE` sync surface to `gs://`/`s3://` (`lib/finelog/rust/src/store/remote.rs`, `store/reconcile.rs`, `store/store.rs`). "Object-store first" means either writing L1+ straight to remote or keeping only an L0 stage — the criterion's own escape hatch. This is the largest behavioral change and where the Grafana-parity risk lives.
- *Per-schema policy framework.* Programmable per-namespace storage and physical partitioning already exist: `rust/src/storage_policy.rs`, `rust/src/partition_policy.rs` (versioned `SegmentPartition { spec_id, values }`, hive-style, additive), plus `ingestion_policy.rs`, `levanter_metrics_policy.rs`, `telemetry_policy.rs`. Secondary indices (trigram/exact/value-counts/covering projections) are described in `lib/finelog/AGENTS.md` under "Secondary indexes." The gap is a single clean *registration* entry point, not the primitives.
- *Client-directed queries.* Missing today. The Python `LogClient` is server-only (`lib/finelog/src/finelog/client/log_client.py`); there is no catalog-fetch + direct-GCS-read path. This is the one genuinely new subsystem: a `GetCatalog`-style RPC exposing segments/indices/partition spec, plus a client planner that resolves against object-store segments.
- *Online migration (MVCC).* A migration framework exists (`rust/src/migrations/mod.rs`, `migrations/telemetry_v1.rs`, `bin/finelog-migrate.rs`) and `spec_id` already makes layout changes additive/queryable across versions. The proposal's versioning + dual-write + query-version flip extends this to partition/index breaks; check whether the current single-`spec_id` model needs an explicit active-ingest-vs-active-query version pointer in the catalog (`rust/src/store/catalog.rs`, which already persists `forward_state`).
- *Legacy GCS cleanup.* One-time archival of pre-policy objects; no maintained-state guarantee for archived data today. Lowest-risk piece, doable as an Iris bulk job as the issue suggests.

**Proposed decomposition (each a reviewable PR, roughly in dependency order)**

1. Policy registration API — consolidate the existing storage/partition/index policies behind one per-schema registration surface; no behavior change, unblocks the rest.
2. Object-store-first writer — remote-canonical L1+ (optional L0 stage) behind a policy flag; validate on `marin-dev` with `telemetry_layout_bench` / `grafana_dashboard_bench` before flipping any prod namespace.
3. Catalog RPC + client-directed reads — new `GetCatalog` and a client that reads segments directly; server query path stays the default.
4. Migration versioning — active-ingest vs active-query version with dual writes and a flip, layered on the existing `spec_id`/migration framework.
5. Legacy archival + maintenance — one-time archival and going-forward GCS hygiene.

Open questions for a human before implementation: (a) L0 staging — keep a local L0 or go fully remote for ingest? (b) does client-directed query need its own authz path, given the server's default-deny auth gate is what protects reads today? (c) catalog freshness/consistency contract for direct client reads against a mutating store.

Refs: `lib/finelog/AGENTS.md` (schema-ownership, indexing, forwarding), `lib/finelog/OPS.md`, and the prior layout work in `.agents/projects/finelog_telemetry_layout/`. Recommend converting the accepted decomposition into tracked sub-issues before coding.

🤖 Research

Finelog currently acknowledges writes after local Parquet and SQLite persistence; [remote sync](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a9a070c2211e920549ea6e168076b2116b1d7d4f/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/remote.rs#L124) archives L1+ Parquet, while [query planning](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a9a070c2211e920549ea6e168076b2116b1d7d4f/lib/finelog/rust/src/query/provider.rs#L103) registers only local files. The repository already has physical [policy primitives](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a9a070c2211e920549ea6e168076b2116b1d7d4f/lib/finelog/rust/src/policies.rs#L22) and a resumable [migration precedent](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a9a070c2211e920549ea6e168076b2116b1d7d4f/lib/finelog/rust/src/migrations/telemetry_v1.rs#L36), but no remotely recoverable catalog, remote query visibility, or versioned table specification. The duplicate-work preflight found no open implementation PR for #8737.

Proposed Fix

Add a dormant object-native path that flushes the existing bounded Arrow buffer to immutable segment objects, publishes one complete namespace catalog per generation, and selects it by conditional `HEAD` update; SQLite and local files become recoverable projections of that catalog. Use one object-aware DataFusion path for server and direct-client execution, with client-side catalog reads, best-effort query reporting, and maximum-query-time MVCC garbage collection. Accept only monotonic `TableSpec` updates and let Finelog automatically dual-write, backfill, verify, and activate them; validate first with `file://` fault tests and disposable copied stores before any marin-dev enablement.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
`levanter.grug._moe` marks the whole package private in its `__init__.py` ("Private Grug MoE backend implementations"), and then prefixes names inside it with an underscore as well. Thirty-seven of those names are imported by a module other than the one that defines them, so the marker says module-private about names that are never used module-privately.

`_zero_inactive_grouped_rows` is the clearest case. It is defined in `_moe/common.py` and used five times in `_moe/sonic_cute.py`, and never in the module that defines it.

The names span thirteen modules:

```
sharding.py                          9    ep_deepep.py                        1
ep_common.py                         9    ep_fixed_all_to_all.py              1
common.py                            6    ep_fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all.py  1
sonic_cute.py                        4    ep_ragged_all_to_all.py             1
cudnn_wgrad_cute.py                  1    ep_ring.py                          1
local.py                             1    scatter.py                          1
sonic.py                             1
```

Some cross a distribution boundary, not just a module one. `lib/marin/src/marin/testing/moe/ragged_ep.py` imports `_clip_receiver_group_sizes`, `_EXPERT_CHUNKS`, `_quack_grouped_gemm_available`, and `_select_expert_mlp` from levanter, and `tests/test_grug_variant_contracts.py` imports `_compact_grug_mesh_shape`. A leading underscore is the only signal Python has for "do not import this", and marin imports them anyway.

The prefix also costs the thing it was meant to buy. Because everything is underscored, the package cannot distinguish a helper genuinely local to one module from one that is part of the package's internal interface. `_moe/sharding.py` and `_moe/ep_common.py` are effectively shared libraries for the backends, and nothing in the naming says so.

Dropping the prefix from names that cross module boundaries inside `_moe/` leaves the package private via its path, which is where privacy is already enforced. It is mechanical: every importer is in this repository, there are no dynamic lookups by name, and the compatibility rule in `AGENTS.md` says to update call sites rather than keep aliases. It is wide, though, which is why it does not belong inside a feature PR — #8549 added six such names by following the surrounding style, and the reviewer noticed the style rather than the change.

Raised in review on #8549: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8549#discussion_r3876485352

Done when:

- Names in `levanter.grug._moe` that are imported by another module no longer carry a leading underscore, and names used only within their defining module still do.
- Importers are updated in place, in `lib/levanter`, `lib/marin`, `tests/`, and `experiments/`, with no compatibility aliases.
- `uv run --no-project infra/ci/run_tests.py` passes, and `./infra/pre-commit.py --all-files` is clean.
issues.title: [levanter] Drop the redundant underscore prefix inside levanter.grug._moe

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
Builds of the patched PJRT wheel in `marin-community/xla` cache `~/.cache/bazel` wholesale, about 11.6 GB against GitHub's documented 10 GB per-repository limit. Retention is unpredictable, and the difference is 1m35s of build time versus 3h31m.

| run | restore | build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [33013385685](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/actions/runs/33013385685) | 3m38s | 1m35s |
| [33093433428](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/actions/runs/33093433428) | 0s, nothing to restore | 3h31m33s |

A save at 2026-08-26T21:12Z was gone by the next build at 2026-08-27T16:29Z, which then paid a full cold compile. A save at 2026-08-27T20:04Z is still present a day later. Both entries are the same size, so exceeding the cap does not by itself explain which one survives.

The cached directory holds more than compile output. `external/` and `cache/repos/` carry fetched repositories including the CUDA 13 redistributables, which cost minutes to download again, while `execroot/.../bazel-out` carries the object files that cost hours to rebuild. No size breakdown has been taken, so which part dominates the 11.6 GB is unknown, and that is the first thing needed.

Impact is bounded. Builds run only on pushes to `main` that touch the wheel, so this costs 3½ hours on a refresh or a build-script change, not on routine work. Promotion runs from a published candidate and never compiles.

Done when:

- a size breakdown of the bazel output base is recorded from a build that runs anyway
- the cached content is small enough to be retained between consecutive builds
- two consecutive builds restore the cache, and the second compiles in minutes rather than hours
issues.title: [xla-fork] Keep the bazel cache small enough to be retained

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
## Problem

PR #7886 introduced a 1,024-snapshot cap for vLLM telemetry. Current `main` keeps the first 1,024 samples in Prometheus exposition order and records the remainder as `sample_limit` drops.

On 2026-08-21, two active serves consistently exceeded that cap:

- 2,610 samples per scrape: 1,024 enqueued and 1,586 dropped (60.8%).
- 1,324 samples per scrape: 1,024 enqueued and 300 dropped (22.7%).

Both reported zero telemetry queue loss. Four smaller serves produced 388–398 samples per scrape and had no sample-limit drops.

Because admission is first-N, metric availability depends on vLLM's exposition order. Adding or reordering upstream metrics can therefore displace existing dashboard metrics without a Marin change.

@rjpower, what contract did you intend for this bound: should the bridge forward every vLLM metric, guarantee a defined metric set, or provide bounded best-effort forwarding? Was 1,024 sized against a representative high-cardinality scrape?

<details>
<summary>Supporting details</summary>

In the same window, five serves exposed all 19 dashboard metric names normally present in the deployed vLLM feed. The capped Gemma serve exposed 10 of 19; these histogram families were absent:

- `inter_token_latency_seconds_{bucket,count,sum}`
- `request_queue_time_seconds_{bucket,count,sum}`

spillover_issues.author: Helw150
spillover_issues.body:
A production v4-2048 job is blocked before its first training attempt. The autoscaler reports 256 healthy VMs, but the scheduler sees only 255 workers in one `tpu-name` group. All 256 tasks remain pending.

This happened on two separate slices:

- `marin-tpu-v4-reserved-2048-us-central2-b-20260827-1951-20cad6fa`
- `marin-tpu-v4-reserved-2048-us-central2-b-20260827-2302-e37ba336`

On the first slice, one host registered as global `worker-0` with blank TPU metadata and collided with another host. In `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py:229`, a missing `tpu_worker_id` becomes worker index `0`. This may cause the collision.

Reproduce:

1. Inspect `/held/iris-run-job-20260827-194841`.
2. Confirm that all 256 child tasks are pending.
3. Inspect the second slice. The autoscaler reports 256 healthy VMs.
4. Group its Iris workers by `md_tpu_name`. Only 255 workers have `t1v-n-7eb9ad44`.
5. Read the job's pending reason: `need 256 workers in same 'tpu-name' group, largest group has 255`.

The first slice was drained and deleted. The replacement produced the same result, which rules out one failed host. Experiment context is in #8734.

Expected: Each TPU VM registers with a unique slice worker ID and complete TPU metadata. A missing `tpu_worker_id` must not silently become index `0`. The scheduler should see all 256 workers in one `tpu-name` group.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Reproduce root cause in worker-id resolution
- [x] Centralize TPU worker-index resolution with fail-fast on blank metadata
- [x] Update all call sites (worker init, infer_worker_id, worker attributes, node-agent telemetry)
- [x] Add regression test
- [x] Lint + tests pass
- [x] Open PR — #8745

**Root cause:** On a TPU slice, worker-index resolution does `int(hardware.tpu_worker_id) if hardware.tpu_worker_id else 0` in four places ([worker.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L233), [infer_worker_id](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/env_probe.py#L353), the [TPU_WORKER_ID attribute](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/env_probe.py#L272), and [node_agent/gcp.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/node_agent/gcp.py#L136)). When the `agent-worker-number` probe returns blank, the host silently takes index `0`, re-registers under the same `{slice}-worker-0` id as the real worker-0, and the slice drops to 255 distinct workers so gang scheduling never reaches 256.

**Fix (#8745):** A single `resolve_tpu_worker_index` helper that raises when the host is on a TPU slice (`tpu_name`/`tpu_type` present) but `tpu_worker_id` is blank, so the worker crashes and re-probes rather than silently colliding. Non-TPU hosts keep index `0`.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
🤖 Manual mitigation restored the slice.

On `t1v-n-7eb9ad44-w-43`, GCP metadata later returned `agent-worker-number=43`. Restarting only its `iris-worker` container caused it to register as slice `worker-43`. Iris then reported 256 distinct worker IDs under one TPU name, and all 256 training tasks entered `RUNNING`.

The fallback from an empty worker index to `0` remains unfixed. Recovery record: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/274

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Evaluate whether June 67B context-extension checkpoints use retained MRCR conversation context when scoring the same final assistant response. The paired evaluator compares `full_context` with `query_only`, scores response-body tokens, and stratifies deterministic bootstrap intervals by needle count and evidence distance.

## Task

An MRCR source document contains two worked examples, a long multi-turn conversation with 2, 4, or 8 relevant facts ("needles"), and a final query. `desired_msg_index` identifies a user request in that conversation; its matching answer is the immediately following assistant message.

Each source row produces two documents with the same final query and gold response:

```text
full_context: two worked examples + target conversation + final query -> gold response
query_only:   two worked examples + final query                       -> gold response
```

The primary two-shot prompt supplies the benchmark's 10-character answer prefix. The evaluator scores only the remaining gold assistant response body. The worked examples, retained conversation, final query, supplied prefix, and EOS are context and receive zero loss. Each condition occupies one unsliced, unpacked sequence.

The paired comparison asks whether retaining the target conversation improves the likelihood of the identical response. Results report `query_only - full_context` NLL and BPB gain, with response-token micro and per-example macro aggregation, sliced by needle count and evidence distance.

### Difference from standard MRCR

Standard OpenAI MRCR gives the model the complete conversation, samples a response, requires the nonce prefix in that response, and grades the generated text with a `SequenceMatcher` similarity score. This experiment instead teacher-forces the gold response and measures its token likelihood twice: once with the target conversation and once without it. The supplied prefix is not scored. The resulting paired NLL/BPB gain is a diagnostic of context use, not an official MRCR generation score, and should not be compared directly with published MRCR scores.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Context gain (`query_only - full_context`) should move from non-positive before extension to positive after 64K/262K adaptation. Fixed qk=1.57 comparisons isolate checkpoint adaptation; qk=1.75 is the deployable final arm.

### Links

- [OpenAI MRCR dataset and task description](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr/tree/f4c69fae7cf81f7ca26b9fee34b392a50f6b8a1d)
- [Research logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/babf963076/.agents/logbooks/paired-mrcr-base-eval.md)
- [Implementation snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/63027b4e72)
- [Final qk1.57 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mrcr-67b-step157000-qk157-cap262144-two_shot-v464cp8ep4)
- [Final qk1.75 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mrcr-67b-step157000-qk175-cap262144-two_shot-v464cp8ep4)

## Results

Context gain is `query_only - full_context`, so positive NLL or BPB gain is beneficial.

| Checkpoint | qk | NLL gain (95% CI) | BPB gain |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| step 141000, pre-extension (8K) | 1.57 | -0.19453 [-0.21900, -0.16930] | -0.05789 |
| step 156000, 64K source | 1.57 | +0.40387 [+0.36399, +0.44537] | +0.12019 |
| step 157000, 262K extension | 1.57 | +1.18860 [+1.14205, +1.23597] | +0.35371 |
| step 157000, deployable arm | 1.75 | +1.26855 [+1.22432, +1.31342] | +0.37751 |

Each checkpoint used the same 299 paired source examples: 598 full-context/query-only condition sequences. Across four checkpoints, this is 1,196 paired checkpoint-example comparisons and 2,392 condition sequences.

Confidence is exploratory because each checkpoint received one evaluation pass over this dataset. One-shot/no-prefix and the full matrix remain untested.

comments.body:

There is no defect described, no affected file/command to repair, and no definition of done — nothing to implement or fix.

What would make a follow-up actionable:
- A concrete change request against the evaluator or experiment code (name the file/module and the desired behavior change), or
- A definition of done for the untested arms the report flags as open — one-shot/no-prefix and the full matrix — e.g. which configs to run and what result gate counts as complete.

Absent one of those, this reads as a tracking record and is best left as-is. Happy to pick it up if you convert it into a specific change or run request.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Added a four-condition oracle-normalized measurement before rerunning the 299-example 262K slice.

The conditions form a 2×2 comparison: needles absent/present and distractors absent/present. `needle_only` retains all repeated target-request turns so the ordinal retrieval problem is preserved; `distractor_only` retains the complementary conversation turns. All four conditions score the same response-body tokens.

The headline recovery ratio is `(distractor_only NLL - full_context NLL) / (query_only NLL - needle_only NLL)`, computed as a token-micro ratio of aggregate paired contrasts. A 10,000-sample bootstrap resamples the same four-condition source tuples within needle-count and evidence-distance strata.

The ratio is identifiable only when the isolated-needle gain is at least 0.10 nats/token, its bootstrap lower bound is positive, at least 99% of bootstrap denominators are positive, and no denominator is zero. Before seeing results, the “good enough” gate is a recovery-ratio 95% lower bound of at least 0.80 plus a positive lower bound for distracted needle gain. Needle-count slices must each have positive distracted needle gain; distance slices are descriptive.

Implementation: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/5c32364665

Next: run the pre-extension checkpoint as a memory/artifact probe on `v4-64-cp8-ep4`, then run the remaining three checkpoints if it succeeds.

comments.body:
🤖 Oracle-normalized MRCR is complete on the same 299-source 262K slice. The clean answer is that the 262K extension retained most of the available needle benefit; the deployable qk=1.75 checkpoint clears the predeclared “good enough” gate with margin.

| Checkpoint | Micro recovery (95% CI) | Micro distracted needle gain (95% CI), nats/token | Decision |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| step141, pre-extension qk=1.57 | 0.13685 [0.12701, 0.14755] | — | negative control |
| step156, 64K source qk=1.57 | 0.48141 [0.45849, 0.50432] | 0.67100 [0.63310, 0.70851] | improved, below gate |
| step157, 262K qk=1.57 | 0.81837 [0.80145, 0.83461] | 1.13309 [1.08808, 1.17825] | passes narrowly |
| step157, deployable qk=1.75 | 0.87094 [0.85895, 0.88223] | 1.21248 [1.16915, 1.25609] | passes |

The preregistered gate was a recovery-ratio 95% lower bound of at least 0.80, an identifiable oracle contrast, and positive distracted needle gain. Both 262K checkpoints pass. The qk=1.75 result retains at least 85.9% of the isolated needle benefit with 95% confidence.

The 2/4/8-needle heterogeneity guard also passes for both final checkpoints: every distracted-needle-gain CI has a positive lower bound. Distance slices are descriptive but consistent with the aggregate result. Qk=1.57 recovery is 0.769/0.767 below 65K evidence distance and 0.842/0.845 in the 65–131K/131K+ bands. Qk=1.75 is 0.847/0.830/0.882/0.894 across the same bands. All distance-band gains are positive with 95% confidence.

Each artifact contains 299 unique source IDs, all four finite condition losses, and 115,834 scored response tokens.
